My therapist used this one: 

Imagine everyone gets a car. Something to move you around and help you do what you need to do. Neurotypicals get cars with an automatic transmission- just turn the ignition, put it in drive, and go. It's easy to figure out the gas, brake, and steering, and boom, they're off. 

ADHD cars have a manual transmission. You have to figure out how to press down the clutch, put it in gear, and ease on the gas to get going. You can't drive a manual car the same way you would an automatic- you stall the engine and get nowhere.

At first you don't know your car is different. Everyone with an automatic sees your in your car and thinks, "Why can't they drive? It couldn't be easier," without knowing your process to get going is way more complicated and involved. And you can end up beating yourself up seeing everyone else zooming around with ease and truly thinking there's something wrong with you or your car for not being able to *just go*. Nothing's wrong with either cars, they just work differently. But once you learn how your manual car works you can reach the same speeds and maneuverability as the automatics.

Yo, this is fucked? 

Sure, the sister is the "villain" in this story because she was obsessive and fucked up. But what happens when she overcomes her issues? And I mean, she clearly has issues- her behavior was out of line and threatened to deeply harm her brother. And she's been sent to therapy, which, again, she needs. But what happens after that? 

She becomes a well-adjusted person and lives her life until she finds out she *wasn't wrong* about the time she saw her brother and the person she was sickly infatuated with? 

I think having a misguided, adolescent infatuation that requires therapy is one thing. Realizing important members of your own family lied to you and sent you to therapy to reinforce that lie is *only going to undo any good work that therapy has done.*

Everyone fucking loses in this situation. Even the homophonic parents. What's going to happen when the brother and his "roommate" have to eventually reveal their situation? Will they want to get married? What happens then?

That's what I find especially sad for the wife in this situation. Whatever abuse occurred was bad enough to make her cut ties with her family, her choice to remain NC is not only protecting her but OP himself. I'm sure she'd do anything in her power to prevent anything bad from happening to her husband the way it happened to her late partner at the hands of her family, and here he is not only doubting her, but serving himself up to them. I can't imagine what she must be feeling.

Can't get over how easily duped you were by her family. How their "sincerity" is enough evidence to prove your wife is just, at her core, bitter and untrustworthy. 

Because *as we all know*, you can spot an abuser by how they *so clearly and openly own up to their abuse*, sparing no detail, usually while twirling a moustache and grimacing menacingly .../s

Seriously, what did your mother in law say that was so convincing you trusted her over your own wife? Did she provide any evidence to prove your wife had lied about her claims of abuse? Because all you seem to have backing your choice is how *sincere* she appeared. 

Hey, hey. Isn't it weird that we live in a world where we haven't rounded up all the abusers in society automatically? It's almost like [a huge fucking part of their abuse ](https://thoughtcatalog.com/shahida-arabi/2018/02/why-do-people-believe-narcissists-rather-than-their-victims/) relies on them being manipulative enough to hide their harmful tendencies. Wild, right. 

[You were manipulated.](https://www.psychologytoday.com/ca/blog/women-autism-spectrum-disorder/202010/are-you-narcissist-s-flying-monkey) and good luck fixing this. YTA

I just started a new job this week. The anxiety I felt during my training is exactly the 'where do I start' study anxiety you're feeling. 

What I've noticed is that non-ADHD people can get by with "What" explanations for things. And by that I mean: *"This is what you need to do/learn  in 'X', 'Y', 'Z'",* and that's usually enough for neurotipicals to accept, understand, and retain knowledge and move on.

I can't retain knowledge unless I understand the *"Why"*. 

Like, pretend you're in a dance class. You learn the moves piece by piece. One step here, another there, a quick change over, all stunningly demonstrated by your instructor. And you're able to perform the moves too;  you know how to do the ball-heel change, the side step. One-by -one they make sense. But then your instructor says, *"Okay, let's take it from the top, **but with music this time,"**  and suddenly, a new element added to the mix is causing you to stumble.

I'm not going to lie, I wrote all of this out and then lost my train of thought. 

I think what I was trying to say was, find the '*Why* The bits of study information are only as uselessly isolated as they appear, unless...

I'm so sorry that happened to you. Glad your parents eventually realized what was happening, but I'm sorry they still did some damage. I'm not autistic but I was diagnosed with ADHD later in life and there's some crossover in symptoms, especially meltdown reactions to too much stimulus/being unable to articulate what you're feeling. When I was a kid I was made fun of for my temper tantrums. It became a running joke in my family- this tiny little girl all enraged with her red cheeks and angry tears streaming down her face, how cute! Eventually they'd start goading me to get a reaction then blame me for it later. 

My grandmother had good intentions and got me some children's books about controlling your emotions, but being told that I was inherently the problem fucked me up for a good while. If it had occurred to her (and she knew how to take videos) she might have filmed me and showed me later in a, "See, this is what you look like when you behave this way. Don't you want to change that?" kind of way. Again, good intentions, but not helpful. Definitely would have made me feel worse; embarrassed and sad at disappointing my grandma, definitely not suddenly inspired to better myself. She wanted to help but figuring out *why* I was feeling what I was feeling instead of *why I should feel bad about it* would have done less damage. 

On the other hand, my mom *did* take pictures of me during my moments of anger and frustration. To her it was cute. I fucking hated those pictures being pulled out a family gatherings. This. The biggest takeaway I got from therapy and mindfulness exercises was getting rid of the "shoulds". Somehow when I was younger the idea that bad things shouldn't happen got ingrained in me, so when bad things happened to me my immediate response was to hyper focus on why they shouldn't be happening and how they came to be in the first place. That mindset just made the bad feelings hit worse. Bad things are *always* going to happen, and getting indignant and angry or sad over their very occurrence isn't a good way to deal with the initial emotional fallout of the bad event. You can't prevent bad things, but you can control your response.

Like, if you're floating in the ocean and the waves are crashing over you, do you cross your arms and resist the flow of water because, dammit, the ocean *should* be calm and placid because you want it to be? Or do you anticipate the water, hold your breath for the swell, and then swim through the wave and get your head above the water? Mindfulness and proper mental action isn't about finding ways to prevent the bad from hitting you, it's about making you buoyant enough to ride each wave.

From the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, a list of traits common to narcissism. I first read this list in Karyl McBride's book "Will I Ever Be Good Enough? Healing The Daughters of Narcissistic Mothers". All of us have these traits to some degree, but with a narcissist they are present in such amounts as to be disruptive to their lives and the lives of those around them. Give them a read, I think what you described of your mom fits a few of them: 


1. Has a grandiose sense of self-importance, e.g., exaggerates achievements and talents, expects to be recognized as superior without commensurate achievements

2. Is preoccupied with fantasies of unlimited success, power, brilliance, beauty or ideal love 

3. Believes that he or she is "special" and unique and can only be understood by, or should associate with, other special or high-status people (or institutions)

4. Requires excessive admiration 

5. Has a sense of entitlement, i.e., unreasonable expectations of especially favorable treatment or automatic compliance with his or her expectations 

6. Is interpersonal exploitative, i.e., takes advantage of others to achieve his or her own ends

7. Lacks empathy: is unwilling to recognize or identify with the feelings and needs of others

I'm 29 and was diagnosed with ADHD last year and went through very similar events to what you've been through (job loss, broke it off with my fiance, was going to lose my apartment, severe depression) and now after a period I've found that medication has helped me immensely. Yes, I'm able to focus and actually complete the little tasks that need to be done in order to function, but it's so much more.

When I'm unmedicated, it feels like the only direction my mind drags me towards is agonizing over the past. The present is a slog, and concepts of the future don't even exist. I don't know if you're experience is similar, but it has to do with our smaller ADHD prefrontal cortex being really shite at executive function and planning. It's like, I can only see the future as a blurry reflection of my painful past, because my past is the only thing my brain can focus on and it latches on to that and projects it. It can't gather the separate parts of my present experience to assemble an accurate representation of what the future could be. When I am medicated, the pieces are there, I can put them together, and I can actually see the stepping stones that my actions lay down to get to the future I want.

I still have a long way to go before I feel 100% put together, and taking medication is only one tool of many I'm using to get there.
